title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon inTextual Graph Soft Prompting

paper.title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting , in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts.
A major development in this line of work is G-Retriever, which combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse . Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever’s graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods to G-Retriever, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt.
We examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model is using graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not actually leverage. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) store knowledge in their parameters, making information outside or newer than their pre-training data hard to access or update ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) . Such external knowledge may be organised as text-attributed graphs ( He et al., 2024 ) . We can incorporate this information into an LLM either by textualizing the graphs , i.e., constructing verbalized descriptions of nodes and edges, or through graph soft prompting , i.e., providing a learned representation generated by a graph neural network (GNN). Verbalisation has two limitations: its token cost grows with the amount of graph content included, and serialisation imposes a sequence order on facts that have no intrinsic order. Expressive Graph soft prompting aims to offer an alternative interface for conveying relational information without verbalising every node and edge. G-Retriever ( He et al., 2024 ) supplies the same underlying graph via both channels. However, this design introduces an identifiability issue: because the graph content is already present in textual form, improvements in answer accuracy alone cannot distinguish whether the model relies on the graph token, the verbalized graph, or both. Furthermore, the training objective does not explicitly enforce that the graph-derived token encodes graph-specific information when the textual channel suffices. Consequently, a token computed from the graph may degenerate into a graph-invariant soft prompt. Figure 1: Graph tokens of all 1,628 WebQSP test questions , projected onto two principal components after removing the mean token 𝝁 \bm{\mu} , with pairwise cosines shown below. G-Retriever interprets its ablations as evidence that the graph encoder and verbalised graph provide complementary graph representations ( He et al., 2024 ) . We revisit this interpretation by testing what the graph token contains and whether the LLM uses it. This study evaluates the proposed mechanism by quantifying both the information encoded in graph-derived tokens and the information that the large language model (LLM) causally exploits during inference. The experimental protocol integrates token-space statistical analyses with fixed-weight causal interventions: individual tokens are substituted with (i) the training-set mean token, (ii) a token sampled from a different example, or (iii) a token recomputed from corrupted or different graph inputs. In addition to answer accuracy, we assess gold-answer log-likelihood to capture subtler shifts in the model’s output distribution, and we employ decoding-based probes to measure the recoverability of question, answer, and graph attributes from internal representations. Graph-free control conditions preserve the projector architecture and the full training pipeline while ablating the graph input itself. Applying this protocol to G-Retriever uncovers an unanticipated phenomenon that we call token collapse , which also recurs in subsequent graph-prompting methods. Specifically, across several graph encoders, benchmark datasets, LLM families, and fine-tuning regimes, the token representations generated by G-Retriever are nearly invariant with respect to the input graph (Figure 1 ). Moreover, substituting these input-dependent projected tokens with a fixed alternative yields no resolved answer-level effect under the default configuration; indeed, a learned constant token that never observes any graph matches or even surpasses the performance of the full model. These results indicate that the collapsed token operates primarily as a soft prompt rather than as a carrier of graph-specific information. Although likelihood-based analyses show that perturbing the token can modulate the output distribution, such sensitivity alone is insufficient to demonstrate input- or graph-conditioned utilization. We associate collapse with two factors: a projector that suppresses variation in the encoder representations and an answer objective that does not require this variation to be preserved. Our ablations implicate both factors, although they do not isolate either as the sole cause. We address them with a two-stage pipeline that first aligns and freezes the graph encoder, then trains separate graph-token and prompt-token pathways. The resulting tokens no longer collapse, but non-collapse alone guarantees neither graph use nor improved accuracy. Depending on the benchmark and training configuration, they may encode the question, an answer prior, graph information made redundant by the text, or graph information that the LLM uses to answer. This distinction matters because task improvements may otherwise be attributed to graph–language alignment even when they arise from the verbalised graph or a graph-independent soft prompt. By separating token variation, graph content, and downstream use, our protocol makes alignment empirically testable and provides concrete criteria for developing graph–language models that preserve and use task-relevant graph information beyond what is already supplied by the textual channel.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: We identify token collapse across G-Retriever benchmarks, graph encoders, LLM families, and tuning regimes, and find the same failure in recent graph-prompting methods. Using matched graph-free controls and fixed-weight interventions, we show that the collapsed token acts primarily as a soft prompt rather than as a graph representation used to answer. We associate collapse with the projector and end-to-end answer training, and propose a two-stage pipeline that mitigates it across the tested settings. Finally, we show that a non-collapsed token may encode question or answer priors , unused graph information , or graph information that changes the answer. Together, these results provide a practical protocol for testing graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Graph soft prompting. Soft prompting conditions an LLM with learned continuous vectors ( Lester et al., 2021 ; Li & Liang, 2021 ) ; graph soft prompting instead projects graph-encoder outputs into one or more such tokens. GraphToken ( Fatemi et al., 2024 ) , GraphLLM ( Chai et al., 2026 ) , GNP ( Tian et al., 2024 ) , GraphGPT ( Tang et al., 2024 ) , and G-Retriever ( He et al., 2024 ) differ in their encoders, token counts, retrieval, and LLM adaptation. In this paper, we test whether G-Retriever and subsequent methods preserve and use graph-specific information in their projected tokens. Evaluating graph–language models. Recent work questions whether existing objectives and benchmarks require graph–language integration. Zhang et al. (2026) show that autoregressive training can favour a text-dominant solution, while Petkar et al. (2026) find that single-modality and raw soft-prompt baselines remain competitive and introduce CLEGR to test compositional graph–text reasoning. We complement these studies by auditing the graph token– LLM interface of graph soft prompting. Extended related work discussion is in Appendix S .

sections.heading: 3.2 The Graph Token Collapse Phenomenon
sections.text: Task accuracy conflates three distinct questions: Does the token vary across inputs? Does the LLM use the graph token? What information does it contain? We address them with complementary measurements of token geometry, fixed-weight interventions, gold-answer likelihood, and decodability. Does the token vary across inputs? We measure inter-sample cosine, the input-specific residual relative to the mean token, and token norm relative to ordinary word embeddings. Collapse appears as cosine near one and a small residual ratio. We also compute inter-sample cosine before projection, on the pooled encoder representations 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} , to determine where collapse arises. Formal definitions are given in Appendix D . Does the LLM use graph-specific token variation? At fixed weights, real uses the original token, mean replaces it with the training-set mean, and swap uses another example’s token. Our main graph-specific intervention, gswap , recomputes the token from another graph while preserving the original question conditioning. node , edge , and rel corrupt individual graph components, while notxt removes the verbalised graph. Retrained no-entity and no-question variants isolate the information available during training. Because accuracy observes only changes in the decoded answer, we also measure the paired change in gold-answer negative log-likelihood under teacher forcing. This detects smaller changes in the output distribution. Full details on our interventions are in Appendix D . What does the token contain? Recoverable content and downstream use are not equivalent: a token may contain information that the LLM ignores. This matters for our pipeline because Stage 1 is conditioned on the question and trained with an answer-related target. A non-collapsed token may therefore encode the question , an answer prediction or prior, the graph , or a mixture . The answer can be a supervision target rather than an input, so it cannot be removed through a fixed-weight intervention; appendix Table 8 maps the information retained by the remaining conditions. We complement the interventions with a post-hoc probe that maps stored tokens to frozen embeddings of the question, answer, or verbalised graph. The map is fitted on half of the test examples; on the held-out half, we report the median rank of each example’s correct target among all candidates. A constant token provides the control rank. Estimation details and limitations are given in Appendix D . Graph-free controls. CONST passes a learned graph-independent vector through G-Retriever’s projector, while MLPQ replaces the graph encoder with an MLP over the question. PT is the raw prompt-tuning baseline, the same as that used by He et al. (2024) , and does not use the projector. These controls distinguish the contribution of graph input from that of token parameterisation.

sections.heading: 3.3 Preventing collapse: a two-stage pipeline
sections.text: Figure 2: Two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 aligns the question-conditioned graph encoder. Stage 2 freezes it and trains separate graph-token and prompt-token pathways. Orange modules are trained; blue modules are frozen. Our ablations associate collapse with two factors: a Sigmoid projector that suppresses encoder variation and end-to-end answer training that does not require this variation to be preserved. We address both while retaining G-Retriever’s data, prompt, answer loss, and optimisation setup (Figure 2 ). Stage 1: preserve input-specific variation. Without the LLM, we train the graph encoder with an InfoNCE objective ( van den Oord et al., 2019 ) . Its pooled representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} is aligned with a frozen embedding of a sample-specific target and contrasted against negative targets. The question conditions each node through 𝐱 v = 𝐳 v + 𝐖 q ​ 𝐪 i \mathbf{x}_{v}=\mathbf{z}_{v}+\mathbf{W}_{q}\mathbf{q}_{i} , with 𝐖 q \mathbf{W}_{q} initialised at zero. We use the answer as the target, or the verbalized graph, when the answer space is too small to distinguish samples (e.g., answers are Yes/No). The encoder is then frozen. Stage 2: separate graph representation from prompting. Using the original answer loss, we jointly train a GELU projector over the frozen encoder and a separate graph-independent prompt token. Freezing protects the variation learned in Stage 1, while the second pathway gives the shared prompting function its own token rather than forcing it to compete with input-specific information. The full objective, targets, and design ablations are reported in Appendix N .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We investigate four questions. RQ1: Do graph tokens collapse, and how general is this behaviour? RQ2: What role does the collapsed token play when the same graph is also verbalised in the prompt? RQ3: What is collapse associated with, and can it be prevented without sacrificing task performance? RQ4: What do non-collapsed tokens encode, and which of that information does the LLM use?

sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: Benchmarks. We use the three GraphQA benchmarks introduced by He et al. (2024) : ExplaGraphs , SceneGraphs , and WebQSP . Following their official splits, retrieval procedures, and evaluators, we report accuracy on ExplaGraphs and SceneGraphs and Hit@1 on WebQSP . Dataset statistics and retrieval settings are in Appendix B . Models. We reproduce G-Retriever with its default graph transformer (GT) and frozen Llama-2-7B ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) . Robustness experiments use GAT, GCN, Qwen2.5-3B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , and LoRA adaptation. Architecture, optimisation, and pipeline settings are in Appendix A . Evaluation stability. Re-evaluating identical WebQSP weights in a separate process changes Hit@1 by 1.04 1.04 points. We therefore require an answer-level difference larger than 2 2 points with p < .05 p<.05 . Gold-answer likelihood is more stable; we require | Δ ​ NLL | > 0.03 |\Delta\mathrm{NLL}|>0.03 and a bootstrap interval excluding the replicate floor. Calibration results are in Appendix D . Statistical testing. Accuracy and Hit@1 comparisons are paired with the exact McNemar test ( McNemar, 1947 ) . We denote p < .10 p<.10 , .05 .05 , .01 .01 , and .001 .001 by † , * , ** , and *** , respectively; unmarked comparisons have p ≥ .10 p\geq.10 . Reported p p -values are unadjusted, so claims rely on the effect-size criteria above and consistent evidence rather than isolated significant cells.

Token cosine ranges from 0.985 0.985 to 0.998 0.998 , while the input-specific residual is only 4–12% of the shared mean, whose norm is 22–97 times that of an ordinary word embedding (Appendix E ). Figure 1 illustrates this geometry on WebQSP . Models with similarly collapsed tokens nevertheless obtain substantially different scores, so task performance does not reveal collapse. The encoder representations are considerably more variable, with cosines between 0.423 0.423 and 0.693 0.693 . This makes GNN oversmoothing ( Rusch et al., 2023 ) an insufficient explanation for token collapse: even if node representations are smoothed within a graph, the pooled outputs might remain distinct across inputs, and near-identity appears only after projection. Collapse also persists across three graph encoders, two LLM families, and frozen and LoRA-adapted LLMs. Moreover, a controlled WebQSP audit finds the same geometry in later single- and multi-token graph-prompting methods (Appendix F ). This answers RQ1 : collapse is a recurring failure mode rather than a peculiarity of one encoder, LLM, or single-token implementation. We next ask what the collapsed token contributes to the answer.

sections.heading: 4.5 RQ4: What does a non-collapsed token carry?
sections.text: Non-collapse shows that tokens differ across inputs, but not what they represent or whether the LLM uses those differences. Because Stage 1 receives the question and an answer-related target, the token may encode the question, an answer prior, the graph, or a mixture. We separate recoverable content from downstream use. sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: What standard evaluation misses. Task accuracy cannot isolate graph-token use, while raw prompt tuning changes the token parameterisation and no-text retraining changes the learning problem. A minimal audit should combine token geometry, a graph-free control using the same projector, and fixed-weight mean , swap , and gswap interventions. The controlled WebQSP audit in Appendix F finds collapse with query-conditioned and multi-token approaches, extending the phenomenon beyond G-Retriever up to most recent graph soft prompting methods. Graph use and accuracy are different outcomes. Our pipeline can make answers depend on graph-specific token variation without improving accuracy. The textual channel may be easier to exploit, while continuous graph tokens may be lossy or difficult for the LLM to interpret. The Qwen2.5-3B results show that this trade-off is not inevitable; alignment claims should therefore report graph use and performance separately. Limitations and future directions. Our detailed analysis covers G-Retriever on three question-answering benchmarks; the cross-method audit is limited to WebQSP , runnable implementations, and controlled variants using G-Retriever’s retrieved subgraphs. The mechanism evidence is associative and does not isolate the projector or end-to-end training as a sole cause. The audited recipe trains from scratch with answer cross-entropy; collapse may differ with pretrained encoders or explicit contrastive, reconstructive, or counterfactual objectives ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Stage 1 explores one alternative, but its conditioning and targets can introduce priors. Gswap tests graph–question pairing rather than fact-level reasoning, and decodability measures recoverability rather than use. Our pipeline is therefore a diagnostic proof of concept. Future work should preserve task-relevant graph information and verify that the LLM uses it.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We uncover token collapse in G-Retriever across benchmarks, graph encoders, LLM families, and tuning regimes, and find the same geometry in controlled tests of later single- and multi-token interfaces. Despite competitive task scores, the projected tokens are nearly identical across inputs. We also find that graph-free controls and fixed-weight interventions match the performance of the original G-retriever model. These findings show that strong task performance can conceal a graph-token interface whose principal contribution is a graph-independent soft prompt, while the verbalised graph provides the dominant graph-information channel. Our two-stage pipeline mitigates this collapse, but also demonstrates that distinct tokens do not guarantee graph use or improved accuracy. Token variation, recoverable graph information, downstream use, and task performance must therefore be evaluated separately. Our protocol provides a practical way to distinguish these outcomes and turns alignment from an architectural assumption into an empirical claim that will foster the development of future graph–language models.

sections.heading: Appendix F Beyond G-Retriever: token collapse in subsequent graph-prompting methods
sections.text: Motivation and scope. We test whether collapse is confined to G-Retriever or recurs in later graph-prompting methods. We consider methods evaluated on WebQSP that construct continuous prompts from graphs and have runnable public implementations. These criteria retain GRAG ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , GRETPool ( Grover et al., 2026 ) , and GraSP ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . We exclude Graph2Token ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , which targets molecular graphs, and GraphAdapter ( Li et al., 2023 ) , which adapts vision–language models. Align-GRAG ( Xu et al., 2025 ) could not be reproduced because its anonymous repository was no longer available. Controlled setup. All methods use the 1,628-example WebQSP test split and the PCST subgraphs retrieved for G-Retriever. Holding retrieval fixed prevents graph size and relevance from explaining differences in token geometry, but makes GRAG-PCST and GraSP-PCST controlled adaptations rather than complete reproductions of the published systems. GRAG-PCST retains the released query-conditioned GAT, projector, and LoRA-tuned Llama configuration. GRETPool uses its reported TopK ( Gao & Ji, 2019 ) and SAG ( Lee et al., 2019 ) ratios of 0.44 0.44 and DiffPool ( Ying et al., 2018 ) budgets of 8 and 100 tokens. GraSP-PCST uses the released SubgraphGNN ( Alsentzer et al., 2020 ) and Graph2Prefix with a local Llama model, producing one token per retained node. Collapse occurs in all six configurations and every tested cardinality: inter-sample cosine is 0.998 0.998 – 1.000 1.000 , and the multi-token methods are also internally almost collinear. GRAG and GRETPool share G-Retriever’s Linear–Sigmoid–Linear projector, so their results show that collapse persists under alternative encoders and pooling operators without changing this bottleneck. GraSP provides the independent case: despite using a Linear–Tanh–Linear projector and one token per retained node, it reaches inter-sample cosine 0.9978 0.9978 , within-example cosine 0.9995 0.9995 , and residual ratio 0.039 0.039 . Its smaller norm ratio ( 4.27 4.27 ) shows that collapse need not involve the unusually large token norms observed with the Sigmoid projectors. Thus, collapse can persist with multiple tokens and with either Sigmoid or Tanh projectors. With the verbalised graph present, none of the direct token-content controls resolves: swap changes Hit@1 by at most 0.921 0.921 points ( p = .298 p=.298 ), gswap by at most 0.676 0.676 ( p ≥ .379 p\geq.379 ), and mean by at most 0.799 0.799 ( p = .263 p=.263 ). Node randomisation is likewise unresolved. Edge rewiring produces two marginal effects: − 1.413 -1.413 for GRAG-PCST ( p = .0616 p=.0616 ) and + 2.088 +2.088 for DiffPool with K = 8 K=8 ( p = .0525 p=.0525 ). Neither satisfies the paper’s joint requirement of | Δ | > 2 |\Delta|>2 and p < .05 p<.05 , and the latter improves rather than degrades performance. The no-text tests use notxt-real , rather than the text-present score, as their paired reference. They provide limited, configuration-dependent evidence: DiffPool with K = 100 K=100 decreases under the mean-token diagnostic ( − 1.904 -1.904 , p = .0472 p=.0472 ), while DiffPool with K = 8 K=8 under swap ( + 2.334 +2.334 , p = .0530 p=.0530 ) and GraSP-PCST under gswap ( + 2.518 +2.518 , p = .0767 p=.0767 ) are marginal. None satisfies both the effect-size and p p -value criteria. Removing the verbalised graph itself lowers performance by 25.6 25.6 – 43.2 43.2 points, but this comparison measures removal of textual evidence rather than graph-token specificity. These results extend the collapse observation beyond G-Retriever: it recurs under GRAG’s query-conditioned single-token method and under fixed, ratio-selected, and node-preserving multi-token pooling. They do not show that every graph-prompting method collapses or that graph information is universally unnecessary. The paired tests establish that token-content replacements are unresolved in every text-present configuration, while the no-text conditions show only limited and inconsistent sensitivity. Because this audit remains single-seed and lacks likelihood measurements, it supports a recurrence claim rather than the stronger conclusions established for G-Retriever in the main experiments. sections.heading: Appendix H Mechanism diagnostics
sections.text: Table 13 supports the first association in Section 4.4 . An untrained projector, at its default initialisation, is applied to 500 random inputs of fixed norm, and the tokens it produces are almost identical to each other unless the input norm is two orders of magnitude larger than anything a trained encoder produces. sections.heading: Appendix K Complete graph-free controls
sections.text: Table 64 gives the controls in full. All four models share G-Retriever’s prompt, answer loss, optimiser and training schedule. const and mlpq also share its projector, so they differ from G-Retriever only in the token’s source; pt differs in both the source and the parameterisation, since its vectors are optimised directly in the embedding space, and its capacity differs by more than two orders of magnitude. ExplaGraphs is the clean test, because its graph is not retrieved: it is the human-annotated explanation graph of the stance, given in full, so an error cannot be blamed on missing information. sections.heading: Appendix S Extended related work
sections.text: Graph soft prompting. A growing line of work connects graph encoders to frozen or adapted LLMs by projecting graph representations into continuous tokens. GraphToken ( Fatemi et al., 2024 ) learns an encoding function that emits soft tokens for a frozen LLM on synthetic graph-reasoning tasks, while GraphLLM ( Chai et al., 2026 ) targets graph reasoning with a tuned decoder and GNP ( Tian et al., 2024 ) adds a cross-modality pooling module for multiple-choice knowledge-graph questions. Among these, GNP and G-Retriever ( He et al., 2024 ) are the only ones that retrieve a question-specific subgraph before encoding; the others operate on the full graph or on synthetic inputs. G-Retriever additionally verbalises the retrieved subgraph in the prompt, creating a redundant configuration that is the focus of our audit. GraphGPT ( Tang et al., 2024 ) combines a text-grounded structural encoder with a lightweight graph–text alignment projector and dual-stage instruction tuning. These systems share the interface we study: a pooled graph representation, a trained projector, and one or a few tokens prepended to the prompt. Multi-token and pooling-based methods. Very few works have explored multi-token methods for graph-to-LLM systems. The single-token bottleneck created by mean pooling over a subgraph has only recently been identified as a structural limitation. Grover et al. (2026) argue that aggressive mean pooling compresses entire graph substructures into a single token, creating a severe information bottleneck, and propose multi-token pooling operators to increase the bandwidth of the graph-to-LLM interface. Their work also reports that pooling methods are unstable under soft prompt tuning with a frozen LLM and require LoRA fine-tuning to stabilise. This is complementary to our diagnosis: we study a single-token approach and show that its collapse is associated with both the projector parameterisation and end-to-end answer training. Graph–language alignment. Alignment-based methods add an auxiliary objective intended to bring graph representations closer to language representations. Align-GRAG ( Xu et al., 2025 ) is closest to our Stage 1: it contrastively aligns a pooled graph representation with a textual target using KL divergence and contrastive losses. G-Retriever ( He et al., 2024 ) can also be viewed as an implicit alignment method, since its projector is trained to map graph representations into the LLM’s embedding space under the answer loss. Our use of contrastive pretraining is similar to Align-GRAG, but our question is different. Similarity between graph and text spaces does not establish that different graphs produce different tokens after projection, nor that the LLM uses their graph-specific content. We therefore complement representation alignment with measurements of token variation and fixed-weight interventions on the trained model. Why graph use is not guaranteed. Two recent works already point out our diagnosis from different perspectives. Zhang et al. (2026) prove that the autoregressive language objective of graph-tokenizing LLMs decomposes into a textual dependency term and a graph–text alignment term, and that current methods optimize only the former explicitly. Graph–text alignment is therefore implicit: the training objective does not reward the model for using graph information, and a text-dominant solution can be optimal under the loss. Petkar et al. (2026) show empirically that existing graph–language benchmarks can be matched by graph-only or language-only baselines, and introduce CLEGR to require compositional reasoning over structure and text; even there, raw soft-prompted LLMs remain competitive with GNN-backed models. Together, these results establish that neither the training objective nor the benchmark forces a model to use graph information. Our work is complementary in level rather than in kind: we study the interface itself and show that a graph token can collapse to a near-constant vector even when the encoder representations are distinct, and that preventing collapse does not guarantee that the LLM uses the token’s graph-specific content. This is what motivates the diagnostic protocol we introduce. Retrieval for graph-grounded generation. G-Retriever ( He et al., 2024 ) formulates subgraph retrieval as a prize-collecting Steiner tree problem ( Bienstock et al., 1993 ) and is the reference implementation we study. GRAG ( Hu et al., 2025 ) retrieves subgraphs for generation with a different scoring rule, emphasising the importance of subgraph structure and topology. GraSP ( Wang et al., 2026 ) encodes subgraphs into soft prompts using GNNs for multi-hop KBQA and combines this with a two-stage LLM reasoning procedure. GNN-RAG ( Mavromatis & Karypis, 2024 ) uses a GNN to retrieve reasoning paths that are then verbalised, rather than projecting them as soft tokens. Retrieval quality is orthogonal to our question: our interventions keep the retrieved subgraph fixed and change only the token computed from it. Parameter-efficient tuning and continuous prompting. Fine-tuning an LLM can be done in several ways. Full-weight fine-tuning updates all parameters. Parameter-efficient methods update a small subset or add new parameters, and include LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , which learns low-rank updates to existing weights, and continuous prompting methods. Continuous prompting conditions a frozen language model with learned continuous vectors. This family includes prompt tuning ( Lester et al., 2021 ) , which learns input-independent embeddings, and prefix-tuning ( Li & Liang, 2021 ) , which learns continuous prefixes made available across the model’s layers. A graph token is a form of continuous prompting, but with a different intended role: it is computed from each input graph and is therefore expected to preserve input-specific information, unlike standard prompt tuning where the prompt is shared across all inputs. Our results connect these settings by showing that Graph Soft prompting, as it is, collapses into a nearly input-independent vector and consequently behaves like a conventional soft prompt. LoRA is used in our work only as a robustness check on the frozen-LLM setting, and the effect is consistent.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.31572v1 [cs.LG] 22 Oct 2026 On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting Andrea Giuseppe Di Francesco 1,2,* Rishabh Jain 3 Franco Maria Nardini 2 Nicola Tonellotto 4 Pietro Liò 3 Fabrizio Silvestri 1 1 Sapienza University of Rome, Rome, Italy 2 ISTI-CNR, Pisa, Italy 3 University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 4 University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy * Corresponding author difrancesco@diag.uniroma1.it Abstract Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting , in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. A major development in this line of work is G-Retriever, which combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse . Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever’s graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods to G-Retriever, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model is using graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not actually leverage. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA . 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) store knowledge in their parameters, making information outside or newer than their pre-training data hard to access or update ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) . Such external knowledge may be organised as text-attributed graphs ( He et al., 2024 ) . We can incorporate this information into an LLM either by textualizing the graphs , i.e., constructing verbalized descriptions of nodes and edges, or through graph soft prompting , i.e., providing a learned representation generated by a graph neural network (GNN). Verbalisation has two limitations: its token cost grows with the amount of graph content included, and serialisation imposes a sequence order on facts that have no intrinsic order. Expressive Graph soft prompting aims to offer an alternative interface for conveying relational information without verbalising every node and edge. G-Retriever ( He et al., 2024 ) supplies the same underlying graph via both channels. However, this design introduces an identifiability issue: because the graph content is already present in textual form, improvements in answer accuracy alone cannot distinguish whether the model relies on the graph token, the verbalized graph, or both. Furthermore, the training objective does not explicitly enforce that the graph-derived token encodes graph-specific information when the textual channel suffices. Consequently, a token computed from the graph may degenerate into a graph-invariant soft prompt. Figure 1: Graph tokens of all 1,628 WebQSP test questions , projected onto two principal components after removing the mean token 𝝁 \bm{\mu} , with pairwise cosines shown below. G-Retriever interprets its ablations as evidence that the graph encoder and verbalised graph provide complementary graph representations ( He et al., 2024 ) . We revisit this interpretation by testing what the graph token contains and whether the LLM uses it. This study evaluates the proposed mechanism by quantifying both the information encoded in graph-derived tokens and the information that the large language model (LLM) causally exploits during inference. The experimental protocol integrates token-space statistical analyses with fixed-weight causal interventions: individual tokens are substituted with (i) the training-set mean token, (ii) a token sampled from a different example, or (iii) a token recomputed from corrupted or different graph inputs. In addition to answer accuracy, we assess gold-answer log-likelihood to capture subtler shifts in the model’s output distribution, and we employ decoding-based probes to measure the recoverability of question, answer, and graph attributes from internal representations. Graph-free control conditions preserve the projector architecture and the full training pipeline while ablating the graph input itself. Applying this protocol to G-Retriever uncovers an unanticipated phenomenon that we call token collapse , which also recurs in subsequent graph-prompting methods. Specifically, across several graph encoders, benchmark datasets, LLM families, and fine-tuning regimes, the token representations generated by G-Retriever are nearly invariant with respect to the input graph (Figure 1 ). Moreover, substituting these input-dependent projected tokens with a fixed alternative yields no resolved answer-level effect under the default configuration; indeed, a learned constant token that never observes any graph matches or even surpasses the performance of the full model. These results indicate that the collapsed token operates primarily as a soft prompt rather than as a carrier of graph-specific information. Although likelihood-based analyses show that perturbing the token can modulate the output distribution, such sensitivity alone is insufficient to demonstrate input- or graph-conditioned utilization. We associate collapse with two factors: a projector that suppresses variation in the encoder representations and an answer objective that does not require this variation to be preserved. Our ablations implicate both factors, although they do not isolate either as the sole cause. We address them with a two-stage pipeline that first aligns and freezes the graph encoder, then trains separate graph-token and prompt-token pathways. The resulting tokens no longer collapse, but non-collapse alone guarantees neither graph use nor improved accuracy. Depending on the benchmark and training configuration, they may encode the question, an answer prior, graph information made redundant by the text, or graph information that the LLM uses to answer. This distinction matters because task improvements may otherwise be attributed to graph–language alignment even when they arise from the verbalised graph or a graph-independent soft prompt. By separating token variation, graph content, and downstream use, our protocol makes alignment empirically testable and provides concrete criteria for developing graph–language models that preserve and use task-relevant graph information beyond what is already supplied by the textual channel. Contributions. We identify token collapse across G-Retriever benchmarks, graph encoders, LLM families, and tuning regimes, and find the same failure in recent graph-prompting methods. Using matched graph-free controls and fixed-weight interventions, we show that the collapsed token acts primarily as a soft prompt rather than as a graph representation used to answer. We associate collapse with the projector and end-to-end answer training, and propose a two-stage pipeline that mitigates it across the tested settings. Finally, we show that a non-collapsed token may encode question or answer priors , unused graph information , or graph information that changes the answer. Together, these results provide a practical protocol for testing graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy. 2 Related work Graph soft prompting. Soft prompting conditions an LLM with learned continuous vectors ( Lester et al., 2021 ; Li & Liang, 2021 ) ; graph soft prompting instead projects graph-encoder outputs into one or more such tokens. GraphToken ( Fatemi et al., 2024 ) , GraphLLM ( Chai et al., 2026 ) , GNP ( Tian et al., 2024 ) , GraphGPT ( Tang et al., 2024 ) , and G-Retriever ( He et al., 2024 ) differ in their encoders, token counts, retrieval, and LLM adaptation. In this paper, we test whether G-Retriever and subsequent methods preserve and use graph-specific information in their projected tokens. Evaluating graph–language models. Recent work questions whether existing objectives and benchmarks require graph–language integration. Zhang et al. (2026) show that autoregressive training can favour a text-dominant solution, while Petkar et al. (2026) find that single-modality and raw soft-prompt baselines remain competitive and introduce CLEGR to test compositional graph–text reasoning. We complement these studies by auditing the graph token– LLM interface of graph soft prompting. Extended related work discussion is in Appendix S . 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries: graph soft prompting in G-Retriever A textual graph G = ( 𝒱 , ℰ , { x v } v ∈ 𝒱 , { x e } e ∈ ℰ ) G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\{x_{v}\}_{v\in\mathcal{V}},\{x_{e}\}_{e\in\mathcal{E}}) associates every node v v with a text attribute x v x_{v} and every edge e e with a text attribute x e x_{e} . Does the LLM use the graph token? What information does it contain? We address them with complementary measurements of token geometry, fixed-weight interventions, gold-answer likelihood, and decodability. Does the token vary across inputs? We measure inter-sample cosine, the input-specific residual relative to the mean token, and token norm relative to ordinary word embeddings. Collapse appears as cosine near one and a small residual ratio. We also compute inter-sample cosine before projection, on the pooled encoder representations 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} , to determine where collapse arises. Formal definitions are given in Appendix D . Does the LLM use graph-specific token variation? At fixed weights, real uses the original token, mean replaces it with the training-set mean, and swap uses another example’s token. Our main graph-specific intervention, gswap , recomputes the token from another graph while preserving the original question conditioning. node , edge , and rel corrupt individual graph components, while notxt removes the verbalised graph. Retrained no-entity and no-question variants isolate the information available during training. Because accuracy observes only changes in the decoded answer, we also measure the paired change in gold-answer negative log-likelihood under teacher forcing. This detects smaller changes in the output distribution. Full details on our interventions are in Appendix D . What does the token contain? Recoverable content and downstream use are not equivalent: a token may contain information that the LLM ignores. This matters for our pipeline because Stage 1 is conditioned on the question and trained with an answer-related target. A non-collapsed token may therefore encode the question , an answer prediction or prior, the graph , or a mixture . The answer can be a supervision target rather than an input, so it cannot be removed through a fixed-weight intervention; appendix Table 8 maps the information retained by the remaining conditions. We complement the interventions with a post-hoc probe that maps stored tokens to frozen embeddings of the question, answer, or verbalised graph. The map is fitted on half of the test examples; on the held-out half, we report the median rank of each example’s correct target among all candidates. A constant token provides the control rank. Estimation details and limitations are given in Appendix D . Graph-free controls. CONST passes a learned graph-independent vector through G-Retriever’s projector, while MLPQ replaces the graph encoder with an MLP over the question. PT is the raw prompt-tuning baseline, the same as that used by He et al. (2024) , and does not use the projector. These controls distinguish the contribution of graph input from that of token parameterisation. 3.3 Preventing collapse: a two-stage pipeline Figure 2: Two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 aligns the question-conditioned graph encoder. Stage 2 freezes it and trains separate graph-token and prompt-token pathways. Orange modules are trained; blue modules are frozen. Our ablations associate collapse with two factors: a Sigmoid projector that suppresses encoder variation and end-to-end answer training that does not require this variation to be preserved. We address both while retaining G-Retriever’s data, prompt, answer loss, and optimisation setup (Figure 2 ). Stage 1: preserve input-specific variation. Without the LLM, we train the graph encoder with an InfoNCE objective ( van den Oord et al., 2019 ) . Its pooled representation 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} is aligned with a frozen embedding of a sample-specific target and contrasted against negative targets. The question conditions each node through 𝐱 v = 𝐳 v + 𝐖 q ​ 𝐪 i \mathbf{x}_{v}=\mathbf{z}_{v}+\mathbf{W}_{q}\mathbf{q}_{i} , with 𝐖 q \mathbf{W}_{q} initialised at zero. We use the answer as the target, or the verbalized graph, when the answer space is too small to distinguish samples (e.g., answers are Yes/No). The encoder is then frozen. Stage 2: separate graph representation from prompting. Using the original answer loss, we jointly train a GELU projector over the frozen encoder and a separate graph-independent prompt token. Freezing protects the variation learned in Stage 1, while the second pathway gives the shared prompting function its own token rather than forcing it to compete with input-specific information. The full objective, targets, and design ablations are reported in Appendix N . 4 Experiments We investigate four questions. RQ1: Do graph tokens collapse, and how general is this behaviour? RQ2: What role does the collapsed token play when the same graph is also verbalised in the prompt? RQ3: What is collapse associated with, and can it be prevented without sacrificing task performance? Task accuracy cannot isolate graph-token use, while raw prompt tuning changes the token parameterisation and no-text retraining changes the learning problem. A minimal audit should combine token geometry, a graph-free control using the same projector, and fixed-weight mean , swap , and gswap interventions. The controlled WebQSP audit in Appendix F finds collapse with query-conditioned and multi-token approaches, extending the phenomenon beyond G-Retriever up to most recent graph soft prompting methods. Graph use and accuracy are different outcomes. Our pipeline can make answers depend on graph-specific token variation without improving accuracy. The textual channel may be easier to exploit, while continuous graph tokens may be lossy or difficult for the LLM to interpret. The Qwen2.5-3B results show that this trade-off is not inevitable; alignment claims should therefore report graph use and performance separately. Limitations and future directions. Our detailed analysis covers G-Retriever on three question-answering benchmarks; the cross-method audit is limited to WebQSP , runnable implementations, and controlled variants using G-Retriever’s retrieved subgraphs. The mechanism evidence is associative and does not isolate the projector or end-to-end training as a sole cause. The audited recipe trains from scratch with answer cross-entropy; collapse may differ with pretrained encoders or explicit contrastive, reconstructive, or counterfactual objectives ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Stage 1 explores one alternative, but its conditioning and targets can introduce priors. Gswap tests graph–question pairing rather than fact-level reasoning, and decodability measures recoverability rather than use. Our pipeline is therefore a diagnostic proof of concept. Future work should preserve task-relevant graph information and verify that the LLM uses it. 6 Conclusion We uncover token collapse in G-Retriever across benchmarks, graph encoders, LLM families, and tuning regimes, and find the same geometry in controlled tests of later single- and multi-token interfaces. Despite competitive task scores, the projected tokens are nearly identical across inputs. We also find that graph-free controls and fixed-weight interventions match the performance of the original G-retriever model. These findings show that strong task performance can conceal a graph-token interface whose principal contribution is a graph-independent soft prompt, while the verbalised graph provides the dominant graph-information channel. Our two-stage pipeline mitigates this collapse, but also demonstrates that distinct tokens do not guarantee graph use or improved accuracy. Token variation, recoverable graph information, downstream use, and task performance must therefore be evaluated separately. Our protocol provides a practical way to distinguish these outcomes and turns alignment from an architectural assumption into an empirical claim that will foster the development of future graph–language models.
